title: Implicit Argument Prediction with Event Knowledge
research_question: Can distributed event knowledge and entity-salience information improve prediction of implicit arguments whose fillers occur elsewhere in a document?
methodology: The paper introduces an argument-cloze formulation in which one argument of an event is removed and the model must select its filler from entities mentioned elsewhere in the document. Event representations are learned from a large English Wikipedia corpus, and a neural coherence model scores candidate entities using event compatibility together with salience features. The model is evaluated on two OntoNotes-derived cloze settings and is additionally adapted to the natural implicit-argument dataset of Gerber and Chai.

key_findings.finding: Combining learned event knowledge with entity-salience features substantially improves argument-cloze accuracy over frequency and simpler event-embedding baselines.
On the shorter OntoNotes setting, the 40-million-example EventComp model with salience reaches 47.75% accuracy, compared with 41.89% without salience and 22.76% for the most-frequent-entity baseline.
On the longer and more entity-dense OntoNotes setting, the 40-million-example EventComp model with salience reaches 27.87% accuracy, outperforming the corresponding model without salience at 21.79%.

For the Gerber-Chai natural implicit-argument task, successive adaptations for deciding whether a role is filled, handling multiple roles, and adding salience raise the 40-million-example EventComp system to 49.6 F1.
key_findings.section: Evaluation on naturally occurring implicit arguments / Table 6

key_findings.finding: The final adapted system approaches the original Gerber-Chai result while exceeding the authors' automatically reproducible Gerber-Chai baseline, suggesting that broad event knowledge can substitute for some manually engineered resources.
key_findings.section: Evaluation on naturally occurring implicit arguments and Conclusion

key_findings.finding: Among the tested salience signals, mention-count information contributes most of the gain, while first-mention location and head-count features provide little or negative additional benefit in the reported ablation.

limitations: The argument-cloze benchmark is synthetically constructed by deleting otherwise explicit event arguments, so it is only a proxy for naturally omitted arguments.
The natural implicit-argument evaluation is small and restricted to ten nominal predicates, limiting conclusions about broader predicate and discourse coverage.
The experiments concern Wikipedia and newswire-style text rather than authentic workplace email or enterprise chat.
The formulation predicts entity fillers for event roles; it does not annotate workplace-specific assignees, group assignees, decisions, deadlines, or action-to-deadline links.
Condition, negation, and modality scope are not represented as target structures.
Candidate fillers are entities/coreference chains rather than arbitrary exact evidence spans, so the task does not directly evaluate exact argument-span extraction.
The natural-task adaptation relies on mapping nominal predicates and semantic roles into the model's verbal/syntactic event representation.
The paper releases code but does not state that its generated cloze instances are distributed as a standalone benchmark dataset.
raw_claims: Implicit arguments are arguments that are not syntactically attached to their predicates but may have fillers elsewhere in the surrounding discourse.
The proposed argument-cloze task removes one event argument and asks a model to recover its entity from the other entities in the document.
The training resources are automatically derived from a large English Wikipedia dump using dependency parsing and coreference information.
The EventComp architecture scores narrative coherence between the event with the missing role and events associated with candidate entities.
Entity salience is represented with features including mention frequency, first-mention location, and head-mention count.
The OntoNotes evaluation uses gold dependency and coreference information to construct controlled argument-cloze cases.
The longer-document test set is harder because each document contains substantially more candidate entities.
Adding salience improves both short- and long-document cloze performance for the EventComp models.
The model must be modified to handle whether an implicit role should be filled and to predict several roles for the Gerber-Chai task.
The best adapted model achieves 49.6 F1 on the Gerber-Chai evaluation.
The authors identify richer global narrative-coherence modeling as a direction for future work.
